query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, dynamic nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries during intermediate-temperature loading reduces the grain boundary cohesive strength, leading to intergranular cracking and brittle failure. Suppressing this nanoclustering via a tailored heat treatment should prevent the embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with a uniform elemental distribution at grain boundaries
generation.intervention: Apply two distinct heat treatments: one that promotes compositional homogeneity and suppresses early-stage elemental nanoclustering at the grain boundaries, and a reference heat treatment that allows the development of nanoclustering
generation.conditions: Perform tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 200–400°C) under constant loading rates, followed by atom probe tomography (APT) analysis of grain boundary chemistry
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary elemental distribution, specifically the degree of nanoclustering (aggregation) of Cr, Ni, and Mn
generation.mechanism: Under intermediate-temperature deformation, intrinsic fluctuations in the multicomponent alloy can drive nanoclustering of selected elements at grain boundaries, which weakens the intergranular cohesion. The tailored heat treatment minimizes these local compositional fluctuations, thereby maintaining ductility. This mechanism is distinct from the conventional alloy behavior where pre‐existing segregation or brittle precipitates govern toughness loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reference specimens (with standard heat treatment) will display significant nanoclustering at grain boundaries accompanied by intergranular cracking and reduced toughness, whereas specimens treated to suppress nanoclustering will retain a more uniform grain boundary composition, exhibit higher toughness, and largely fail via transgranular mechanisms.
generation.baseline: The initial state is a single-phase, compositionally complex HEA known to experience ductility loss at intermediate temperatures, previously correlated with grain boundary nanoclustering.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under intermediate-temperature conditions (200–400°C). At very high temperatures, nanoclusters may dissolve, and at cryogenic temperatures other deformation mechanisms may dominate, so the hypothesis is bounded to service conditions resembling the prescribed testing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative contribution of nanoclustering relative to other potential microstructural changes induced by the heat treatments (e.g., grain size variations or residual stresses), which might also affect toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA specimens using distinct heat treatments: one designed to suppress early nanoclustering and a reference treatment that allows its development. Subject both sets to tensile testing at intermediate temperatures (200–400°C) under identical loading conditions, then perform atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify grain boundary elemental distributions. Correlate the mechanical performance (specifically toughness and fracture mode) with the extent of nanoclustering.
measurements: Fracture surface analysis (e.g., SEM) to determine intergranular vs. transgranular cracking
Quantitative assessment of nanoclustering at grain boundaries using APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored heat treatment specimen and the reference specimen show similar degrees of nanoclustering at the grain boundaries and comparable mechanical toughness (with no significant shift from intergranular to transgranular fracture mode), then the hypothesis that nanoclustering drives brittle behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. proposals.intervention: Apply two distinct heat treatment routes – one that promotes homogeneity and suppresses any early-stage elemental nanoclustering at grain boundaries, and a reference treatment known to permit nanoclustering.
proposals.conditions: Perform tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 200–400°C) under identical loading rates, followed by atom probe tomography (APT) analysis of grain boundary chemistry.
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain boundary elemental distribution, particularly the degree of nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn.
proposals.mechanism: Under service-like loading at intermediate temperatures, intrinsic local fluctuations in the multicomponent alloy can drive nanoclustering of specific elements at the grain boundaries, thereby reducing the cohesive strength of the boundaries and promoting brittle intergranular fracture. Suppressing such clustering by a tailored heat treatment should prevent the embrittlement.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The reference (unmodified) specimen will exhibit pronounced grain boundary nanoclustering and reduced toughness via intergranular cracking, whereas the homogeneously heat-treated specimen will retain ductility with a more uniform elemental distribution at GBs.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction directly tests whether toughness degradation in an initially single‐phase HEA arises from dynamic grain boundary chemistry evolution (nanoclustering) under load, distinguishing it from conventional alloy behavior that typically involves pre‐existing segregation or precipitates.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor molybdenum addition (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25) while maintaining a single-phase solid solution via controlled melting and homogenization.
proposals.conditions: Subject both the baseline and Mo-alloyed HEAs to high-temperature aging (e.g., 650°C) followed by tensile deformation tests to assess ductility loss and fracture mode.
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and the emergent tendency toward segregation or nano-precipitate formation.
proposals.mechanism: The addition of Mo is expected to alter the energetic landscape for solute distribution along the grain boundaries. In the baseline alloy, subtle local compositional fluctuations might trigger ductility loss, whereas Mo’s presence should retard or modify such segregation, thereby delaying brittle behavior.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The Mo-containing alloy will show delayed onset of brittle intergranular fracture and improved toughness under high-temperature loading compared to the base alloy, as confirmed by reduced evidence of grain boundary segregation via microscopy and APT.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This comparison tests whether modifying internal solute interactions in a compositionally complex alloy changes the onset of brittle failure – a phenomenon not governed by conventional grain-boundary precipitation but by dynamic changes in local chemistry.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM)
proposals.intervention: Vary the cooling rate of post-SLM solution heat treatment to induce two different grain boundary morphologies: one with straight boundaries (fast cooling) and one with serrated boundaries (slow cooling).
proposals.conditions: Conduct tensile and creep tests (e.g., at 650°C) on samples with both grain boundary morphologies, and use microstructural and strain mapping analyses.
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology (straight versus serrated boundaries that promote distributed strain).
proposals.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries offer enhanced distribution of local stresses, making them less prone to stress concentration–induced brittle cracking. If brittle behavior in single-phase HEAs stems from localized strain accumulation at otherwise ‘clean’ boundaries, a serrated morphology should mitigate this effect.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples possessing serrated grain boundaries will exhibit higher fracture strains and longer creep rupture lives. In contrast, the straight-boundary samples will show earlier onset of brittle intergranular failure, indicating a sensitivity to local strain concentrations.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This controlled comparison isolates the effect of grain boundary architecture on toughness degradation in HEAs, allowing the hypothesis that dynamic strain accommodation via boundary serration delays brittle failure to be decisively tested.

proposals.intervention: Perform high strain-rate deformation tests at different temperatures (e.g., room temperature versus cryogenic conditions) while monitoring in situ microstructural evolution (e.g., twin formation and dynamic adiabatic heating effects).
proposals.conditions: Employ controlled high strain-rate tensile tests with simultaneous high-speed imaging or in situ TEM at varying temperatures, from cryogenic (~-196°C) to ambient, to capture twin nucleation and adiabatic heating effects.
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation/distribution of deformation twins and any associated local adiabatic heating-induced microstructural changes (such as local segregation at twin boundaries).
proposals.mechanism: At intermediate to high strain-rates, competing mechanisms—namely, deformation twinning (which enhances local strain hardening) and adiabatic heating (which may promote local compositional reordering or depletion)—are hypothesized to influence the transition from ductile to brittle behavior. At cryogenic temperatures, where adiabatic effects are minimized, twins dominate and enhance toughness; whereas at room temperature or above, adiabatic heating could trigger local compositional anomalies that reduce ductility.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Cryogenic tests will show extensive twin formation with enhanced toughness and ductility, while room-temperature high strain-rate tests will reveal evidence of localized microstructural changes (e.g., elemental rearrangement at twin or grain boundaries) and a propensity toward brittle failure. A decisive falsification would occur if no significant difference in failure mode is observed across the tested temperature range.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach probes whether dynamic, deformation-induced microstructural and chemical changes—unique to the complex alloy system rather than classical precipitate formation—govern the brittle transition in single-phase HEAs during service-like loading conditions.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. This direction directly tests whether grain boundary morphology (serrated vs. straight) governs toughness degradation in an initially single‐phase HEA by isolating its effect on local stress distribution.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraint by using a compositionally complex CoCrFeMnNi alloy processed by SLM and evaluates behavior at 650°C without introducing extraneous phases.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism—serrated grain boundaries distributing strain more evenly to delay intergranular cracking—is physically sound and supported by both experimental results and MD simulations.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible with established heat treatments, tensile/creep testing, and microstructural analyses.
critiques.evidence: The supplied evidence from PMC9848264 (records PMC9848264::web::021, PMC9848264::web::000, PMC9848264::web::020) supports the role of serrated grain boundaries in increasing ductility and creep life.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that varying the cooling rate may not exclusively modify the grain boundary morphology but could also inadvertently alter precipitate size/distribution, complicating the isolation of the morphology effect.
critiques.fix: Include a detailed characterization and control of precipitate evolution to ensure that the only variable affecting toughness is the change in grain boundary morphology.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It tests the hypothesis that dynamic grain boundary nanoclustering of elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) reduces cohesive strength, leading to brittle intergranular failure in HEAs.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraint by maintaining a CrMnFeCoNi HEA and subjecting it to controlled heat treatments and intermediate temperature tensile tests.
critiques.physical_soundness: The proposed mechanism is physically plausible given that nanoclustering can weaken grain boundaries, as supported by atom probe measurements.
critiques.feasibility: The methodology (varying heat treatments, performing tensile tests, and employing APT) is achievable with currently established techniques.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC6897545 (PMC6897545::web::000 and PMC6897545::web::008) supports the notion of nanoclustering-induced embrittlement in HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the heat treatment intended to suppress nanoclustering might also alter other microstructural features (e.g., grain size or residual stresses), thus confounding the attribution of toughness changes solely to nanoclustering.
critiques.fix: Implement complementary microstructural characterizations (e.g., grain size analysis and residual stress measurements) to isolate and quantify the effect of nanoclustering on grain boundary cohesion.

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially. The direction tests whether modifying the alloy chemistry via minor Mo addition can alter the local solute distribution at grain boundaries to delay brittle behavior. However, it may not directly capture the dynamic mechanisms underlying toughness degradation in a truly single-phase HEA.
critiques.constraints: While it maintains a compositionally complex AlCoCrFeNi system, the introduction of Mo may risk altering the phase stability by potentially triggering secondary phase (e.g., σ phase) formation.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis that Mo alters the energetic landscape to retard harmful segregation is plausible, but the risk of forming additional phases complicates the expected behavior.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible using standard melting, homogenization, aging, and tensile testing procedures alongside microscopy and APT.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC12525669 supports Mo addition effects in similar systems, though it also indicates possible σ phase formation that may impact ductility.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the addition of Mo could destabilize the single-phase character of the alloy by inducing secondary phase formation, thereby affecting toughness through unintended mechanisms.
critiques.fix: Reduce the Mo content further and perform rigorous phase stability assessments to ensure that the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution without the formation of deleterious secondary phases.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. This direction hypothesizes that the competition between deformation twinning and adiabatic heating-induced local compositional changes governs the brittle transition in a refractory multi‐principal element alloy.
critiques.constraints: It complies with the constraint by using a compositionally complex RMPEA (NbTaTiV) under service-like conditions at different temperatures and strain rates.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; twin formation can indeed influence strain hardening while adiabatic heating under high strain rates can reduce ductility. However, disentangling these effects can be challenging.
critiques.feasibility: The method, including high strain-rate tests with in situ TEM or high-speed imaging across a temperature range, is challenging but feasible with modern experimental setups.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC12463061 (PMC12463061::web::000, PMC12463061::web::025, PMC12463061::web::032) supports the sensitivity of RMPEA mechanical behavior to both twin formation and adiabatic heating effects.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the interplay between twin formation and adiabatic heating may be difficult to isolate, making it challenging to decisively attribute brittle behavior to one mechanism versus the other.
critiques.fix: Incorporate complementary diagnostics (e.g., localized temperature measurements or thermal imaging) during high strain-rate tests to clearly distinguish the contributions of adiabatic heating from those of deformation twinning.
